newsitem.title: INDIA: India Thermax launches export thrust.
newsitem.headline: India Thermax launches export thrust.

text.p: Spurred by bad times at home, Indian energy and environment management company Thermax Ltd is gearing up for an ambitious thrust to boost exports to $100 million by the year 2000.

"Our exports last year were $20 million," Abhay Nalawade, managing director of the 5-billion-rupee-turnover firm, told Reuters at his headquarters in the western city of Pune, 200 kilometres (125 miles) from Bombay.
"We're really hoping in three years we can reach $100 million," Nalawade added. But quadrupling the company's exports called for a massive effort, he said.
"It comes down to shaking up the entire organisation to tell them it's survival of the fittest."
At home, Thermax plans to tap India's huge water purifier market, which it sees bringing it one billion rupees ($28 million) in annual revenue by 2000.
Thermax's joint venture with American water treatment major Culligan Water Technologies Inc., in which the two are equal partners, will launch its first products this month.
In recent months, Thermax has restructured and slimmed down to tighten focus on its core business of boilers, heat recovery systems, chillers, chemicals and pollution control equipment.
Its forays into exports will see it widen its networks to include Latin America, East Africa and Australia, in addition to present operations in Europe, south-east Asia and Russia.
"We see south-east Asia, and the Middle East as good markets," Nalawade said. "Other markets are developing here and there -- Turkey, or Oman, or Iran, are also good markets."
An industrial slowdown, coupled with the death of its founder and labour problems that forced the shut-down of some plants gave Thermax a difficult time last year.

It was the first time this decade that Thermax reported a drop in net profit, of roughly four percent to 431.6 million rupees for the financial year 1996/97 (April-March), compared with 451.7 million the previous year.
Nalawade attributed the drop to the slowdown, which he said had forced many industrial houses to put new projects on hold.
"There was a slackening of demand so far as new projects, medium- and small-size are concerned," Nalawade said.
"Some major projects we had on hand were held up. The sum total is our turnover grew by about 11 percent, and profits dropped by about 4 percent," he said.
But the company remains a favourite of analysts and investors, who saw the problems as temporary.
"Funds had already been allocated to manufacturing units before the economic depression began to show," said an analyst with a Bombay-based investment house.
"So by virtue of its product and service, the company did not get affected by the slowdown till late last year."
Thermax was set up to manufacture baby boilers under the name Wanson India in 1967. It ended its first year of operations with an income of four million rupees.
Today its manufacturing facilities are spread over 14 plants at four locations, it employs 2,700 people, and has a turnover of five billion rupees.

Nalawade plans to achieve his export target in the same way as Thermax has grown over the years -- through strategic alliances with strong local players which will give Thermax a foothold in overseas markets.
Thermax Culligan Ltd, a 50/50 joint venture set up in May, is intended to bring every water purification technology into the country, Nalawade said.

"We're entering with reverse osmosis, ultrafiltration, ozonisers -- all the options," he said. "I mean comprehensive reach, like the Thermax boiler range -- every boiler, every size, every fuel, every design."

Thermax's joint venture with Japan's Fuji Electric Ltd to make process control equipment in India has just completed its first year of real performance, Nalawade said, with a turnover of 50 million rupees.
Fuji has a 49-percent stake in Thermax Fuji Electric Ltd.
"It is the first company to make 100 percent indigenous instrumentation transmitters in the country," Nalawade said. "It will have a capacity to produce 40,000 units annually."

Thermax's oldest joint venture, the ten-year-old Thermax Babcock Wilcox, in which American firm Babcock and Wilcox has a 40 percent stake, makes industrial boilers and contributes about one billion rupees annually to the group's turnover.
